newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military unveils stealth fighter for next century.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military unveils stealth fighter for next century.

text.p: The U.S. Air Force was scheduled to unveil its new stealth fighter plane for the next century on Wednesday, billing the controversial F-22 as the most advanced fighter in the world.

In a joint ceremony with aviation giants Lockheed Martin and Boeing and engine maker Pratt and Whitney, owned by United Technologies Corp, the Air Force planned a theatrical roll-out for the sleek, twin-tailed craft, which its makers said was designed "to secure air dominance over any adversary aircraft."
The multi-million dollar F-22, also known as the Raptor, "will help preserve the United States' military advantage, and therefore U.S. security, well into the 21st century," Lockheed Martin said.
Stealth aircraft present a minimal radar profile to enemy radars, enabling them to ghost towards their targets and destroy them while remaining virtually invisible to electronic surveillance.
In a crossover between the defence and entertainment industries, an F-22 flight simulator was presented on the eve of the roll-out by computer game maker Interactive Magic.

Company officials said Lockheed Martin had collaborated closely in the design of the simulator, which offered armchair fighter buffs a chance to test the plane's touted capabilities by shooting down "enemy" craft from a great distance without being seen.
In the real world, though, the F-22 has come under cost pressure, just as the Defence Department is reviewing whether U.S. defences need all the planes and other weapons now planned.
A Pentagon analyst group concluded early this month that plans to buy 438 F-22s could cost $16 billion more than the Air Force's $71 billion estimate.
Defence Secretary William Cohen told Congress in a letter that if costs do go up the number of planes will be cut or costly features dropped or both "to keep the programme stable and affordable."
But for now, Cohen said, he would stay with the $71 billion Air Force estimate. Both the Air Force and Lockheed Martin say they are taking steps to prevent the $16 billion increase.
Cohen said the possible cost increase will be taken into account in the current comprehensive Quadrennial Defence Review of what weapons and programmes are required for U.S. defence needs.

The Congressional Budget Office questioned in a report whether the military can afford what it estimated would be a $350 billion cost for all three new planes now planned -- the Air Force F-22, the Navy F/A-18E/F and a Joint Strike Fighter for all services.
Gen. Joseph Ralston, vice chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, told Congress the four-year review will consider a range of options, including scrapping one of the three new planes.

The analyst report, by the Cost Analysis Improvement Group in Cohen's office, did not say the $16 billion could increase the total cost to $87 billion, but that it could raise the $48 billion production part of the Air Force $71 billion estimate to $64 billion.
